tagline: Mining towns and a mountain spur between Santa Fe and Albuquerque
intro: The Turquoise Trail follows NM 14 through rock outcrops and hills dotted with piñon and juniper between Santa Fe and the country east of Albuquerque. The National Scenic Byway also includes NM 536, a winding spur to Sandia Crest. The Federal Highway Administration highlights the Cibola National Forest, Sandia Mountain Wilderness and the artistic communities of Madrid and Los Cerrillos.

The numbered road has its own history: NM 10 connected Albuquerque and Santa Fe before 1927. In 1970, the state reused the NM 14 number for NM 10 to avoid confusion with Interstate 10. In 1988, the section south of Tijeras was renumbered again, becoming NM 337 and NM 55. The mountain branch developed separately: the Forest Service completed a dirt road to Sandia Crest in 1927, and paving in 1960 improved access to the ski area.

The byway’s name comes from local turquoise deposits. Other minerals shaped its towns: Golden grew after an 1825 gold discovery, while Madrid’s coal business declined as home heating and locomotives changed fuels.

Traveling south from Santa Fe, visit Los Cerrillos, then Madrid and Golden before reaching San Antonito’s junction with NM 536. The Crest is a separate excursion; return to NM 14 for Cedar Crest and the finish at Tijeras beside I-40.

moments.title: Madrid
moments.text: Madrid’s miners’ cabins arrived in pieces by rail, some from as far away as Topeka, Kansas. Local carpenters and suppliers could not provide the buildings quickly enough for the new coal town. Corporations owned Madrid for 80 years after its 1895 founding celebration; the town never incorporated. Natural gas displaced coal for home heating, and the railroad replaced coal-burning steam locomotives with diesel-electrics. When coal demand fell, the Albuquerque and Cerrillos Coal Company ceased operating in 1954 and most residents left. Galleries now line NM 14, while black piles of mine waste remain on the hillsides above the miners’ cabins.
moments.notice: Black mine-waste piles remain on the hillsides above rows of miners’ cabins.

moments.title: Golden
moments.text: Gold was discovered here in 1825, before the California and Colorado rushes. The first placer finds came from Tuerto Creek on the southwest side of the Ortiz Mountains and gave rise to two mining camps. Golden, formally established in 1879, absorbed both camps and became the district’s center, with saloons, a school and a stock exchange. The post office closed in 1928 as the population dwindled. San Francisco Catholic Church was restored by Fray Angelico Chavez in 1960; ruins and mining remnants lie across the highway, west of the church.

moments.title: Sandia Crest
moments.text: NM 536 winds to a viewing area on Sandia Crest, a long ridge with a steep western face above Albuquerque. The range drops more than 4,000 feet in two horizontal miles toward the Rio Grande Valley, while its eastern slope descends more gently. The Forest Service finished a dirt road here in 1927; paving followed in 1960 to improve access to La Madera Ski Area. The tramway reaches a different point on the crestline, south of Sandia Crest at the ski area. Spruce and fir cover much of the Crest, where radio and television antennas share the ridge with the viewing area.
moments.notice: The ridge slopes gently east and drops sharply west toward Albuquerque.
